headline.main: Right Wing Report: How Germany's AfD Intends to Boost Its Influence
headline.social: Right Wing Report: How Germany's AfD Intends to Boost Its Influence

intro: By the time Germany's next elections roll around, the right-wing Alternative for Germany party hopes to be the country's strongest political power. Voter frustration is helping, but does the party actually have a plan?
text:
The man standing in Zur Daisy, a bar in the small town of Güstrow, just south of the Baltic Sea coastal city of Rostock, can hardly believe his luck. It is a recent Monday evening and the smell of cigarettes hangs thick in the air. Around three dozen men and a couple of women have turned up for a regular gathering of local AfD supporters, glasses of beer or shots of schnapps on the table in front of them, and they are listening to Christoph Grimm, who was recently elected to German parliament as a candidate from the right-wing populist party. He is gushing about his new life in the Bundestag.
"The food is great,” he says. "The very best quality!”
And the chauffeur service – amazing. Just a single call and the driver shows up within 15 minutes. "It’s a fantastic perk.”
What’s more, says Grimm, you have considerable resources at your disposal. He says he wants to be completely transparent, adding that it’s publicly available information anyway. He receives a salary of over 11,000 euros per month, he says, along with another 25,000 euros per month for staff. He’s already hired one employee, he adds.
What political goals does he hope to achieve with all that funding? That is something his listeners do not learn on this particular evening. Instead, he talks about his great excitement about finally having made it to Berlin, the epicenter of German political power.
A 68-year-old lawyer, Grimm used to be a member of the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), but he left the party in 2013, disgusted by the efforts to save the European common currency, the euro. He was among the founding members of the Alternative for Germany in the state of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, and in February elections, he won a direct mandate in his electoral district. He is now one of 152 AfD members of parliament in Berlin, 69 more than in the last legislative period.
In late March, as the new Bundestag gathered for its first post-election session, it was clear for the first time what this figure means and the effect it will have in the coming years. The AfD, seated to the right of the Christian Democrats and Christian Social Union – a center-right alliance known as the Union – makes up the second largest group in the plenary hall, a powerful bloc that sought to drown out speakers from other parties with heckling, derision and contempt. A bloc that seemed to be bursting with confidence, just as Grimm was in Güstrow. After all, the party is once again on the rise, or so it seems.
Indeed, the AfD’s polling numbers have not receded since the election. On the contrary, while the right-wing extremist party won 20.8 percent of the vote in February, it is now polling between 21 and 24 percent in nationwide surveys, depending on the institute. And it is creeping closer and closer to the Union.
That fact hung like a cloud over the just-completed coalition negotiations between the Union and the SPD. Particularly when it comes to the big issues of migration, finances, war and peace, the negotiators not only had to consider what their decisions would mean for the country and for the voters. But also for the future prospects of the AfD.
Those prospects will likely depend heavily on the next government. Will the Union-SPD coalition, under the leadership of soon-to-be chancellor Friedrich Merz, be able to reestablish trust in the political center and thus erode AfD support? Or will the next elections – which will be held in 2029 at the latest – see the AfD emerge as the most powerful political party in Germany? Might Germany’s next chancellor even come from the right-wing party?
Merz’s coalition with the SPD is the last chance for the political center – at least that’s what everybody is saying. It is a view that has become widely accepted. But is it true?
The answer to that question won’t just depend on the Christian Democrats, the Christian Social Union and the Social Democrats. It won’t just depend on how they govern the country in the coming years. It will also depend on the AfD itself. The question is how the party intends to use the coming years and what strategy it plans to follow between now and 2029.
A Meeting with the AfD's Éminence Grise
It's a recent Tuesday evening in an Italian restaurant in Potsdam, the town just outside of Berlin that also serves as the capital city of the state of Brandenburg. Piano music is playing quietly in the background. Alexander Gauland, the honorary head of the AfD, is well-known here and the personnel greet him warmly by name. The waitress seats him near the door, well aware that it is his preferred table.
Gauland left the CDU in 2013 after four decades of membership, and since then, it has been his goal for the AfD to catch up to the center-right party and even pass it. Just before the meeting in the Italian restaurant, his office manager informed him that has just come one step closer to that goal, with the most recent survey conducted by the pollsters at Forsa indicating that the AfD is just a single percentage point behind the CDU. But Gauland is unimpressed. "That is just a momentary snapshot,” says Gauland, who was once chair of the party. "It’s not a law of nature that we will exceed the CDU in the next election.”
Not a law of nature. It is quite a statement when you think about it. Just a couple of years ago, Gauland would have been laughed out of the room had he said such a thing. Back then, it was completely unimaginable that the AfD would ever come anywhere close to the Union in nationwide elections.
Gauland likes to present himself as a middle-of-the road conservative, someone who is merely trying to force the CDU – which slid to the left under Angela Merkel’s leadership – back to the right again. But it was also Gauland who integrated right-wing extremists like Björn Höcke from Thuringia into the AfD and made them acceptable. And it was Gauland who described the Nazi dictatorship as "nothing but a spot of bird shit on over 1,000 years of successful German history.” And who announced he was planning on "hunting down” the federal government following the 2017 elections.
His voice still carries weight in the AfD, and he is seen as one of very few in the party who takes the long view. What does he think will happen with the party over the next several years? How does he think the AfD should position itself?
The AfD, he says, must do everything it can to embarrass the CDU. "We will put CDU demands up for vote in the Bundestag, particularly when it comes to issues like migration.” The CDU, of course, will be unable to support proposals coming from the AfD, which will – according to Gauland’s calculus – serve to further erode the center-right’s credibility.
Hunting down the CDU, essentially. Only this time, he doesn’t say so explicitly.
Gauland says that if Germany’s next chancellor, almost certainly to be CDU leader Friedrich Merz now that coalition negotiations have been successfully completed, is unable to revive Germany’s economy and get migration under control, then the center-right’s poll numbers will continue to sink.
"CDU members will see that Merz, in a coalition with the SPD, will not be able to implement the policies he has promised,” says Gauland. He hopes that the realization will provoke an uprising among CDU supporters. Large number of CDU voters, Gauland believes, could ultimately prove willing to create majorities together with the AfD.
Majorities for what, though? As the evening progresses, it is striking how little Gauland has to say about his own party’s program and about what the AfD hopes to achieve for Germany. Instead, he focuses his attention on others, particularly the CDU, and on how the AfD hopes to put the conservatives under pressure and force them into a corner.
When the conversation does turn to the AfD, Gauland talks about what the party shouldn’t do, what it must avoid. "I hope that our people are smart enough to moderate their tone such that middle-class voters are not turned off,” he says.
Is that a plan? It is the beginnings of a plan, at least, one which contains the same three elements you hear from party leaders: destruction, discipline, patience. In other words: All we have to do to achieve our goals is wait for the others to make mistakes and keep our composure.
But can that really work?
A look to the state of Saxony-Anhalt is instructive. The AfD state chapter there has been classified by German security officials as right-wing extremist. And the party won every single electoral district in the state, both in rural areas and in large cities home to universities. In many cases, they did so with candidates who likely would have been complete non-starters had they belonged to other parties.
Volker Scheurell from Wittenberg is one example. A carpenter by training who appeared on his campaign posters in work clothing, Scheurell’s most recent job was as a janitor. Had he been a candidate for the CDU or SPD, he would almost certainly have been the focus of a fair amount of negative attention and cost the party a couple of percentage points. Credibility, after all, is the primary currency of election campaigns. But Scheurell won his electoral district over the CDU candidate with 10 percentage points to spare.
Or the dentist Christina Baum, who lives in the southern German state of Baden-Württemberg and has no connection whatsoever to her electoral district in the Harz mountains. Normally, such a shortcoming would not sit well with voters, but Baum beat her CDU competitor by 15.5 percentage points.
Or Claudia Weiss, 50, from Bernburg an der Saale. She won direct election in the state capital of Magdeburg. She worked for a time as a service manager in care homes before becoming a spokesperson for the AfD state parliamentary group in 2019. She told the local newspaper, the Volksstimme, that her priorities are "genuine educational opportunities, social justice and a strong Germany,” a sentence oozing with banality and one that could have come from the mouth of any SPD candidate.
So if the AfD’s candidates are clearly not the party’s recipe for success, what is it?
The Strength of the AfD in the East
It’s a Thursday evening in March in the town of Luckau, located southeast of Berlin in the state of Brandenburg, and just 11 people have turned up for the SPD’s regular gathering in the dimly lit Pizzeria Continentale. The focus of the evening’s discussion is the "federal elections and its consequences” for the local region.
In February’s general election, the SPD only received half as many votes in Brandenburg as it did in 2021, while the AfD result came close to exceeding the CDU and the SPD put together. The mood in the pizzeria matches the lighting, with somber faces surrounding a table weighted down with food, beer and mineral water. It almost feels like a conspiratorial meeting of an underground resistance group.
Why is the AfD so successful here? "Because they are always there,” says the meeting’s organizer, the SPD state parliamentarian Nadine Graßmel. The AfD is extremely active in the region, she says, constantly organizing gatherings at the local pub, film evenings and discussion groups. The SPD, on the other hand, lacks sufficient supporters and visibility in the sprawling electoral district. "We’re just tiny clusters here and there,” says Graßmel.
Still, ideas are plentiful. One participant, who recently left the Green Party but hasn’t yet become a member of the SPD, wants to remove right-wing extremist stickers in the region, start a choir in her village, develop a ride-share app, open a kind of village cafeteria and start a youth club. Nobody has a clue where the money for such projects should come from, but they all agree that they have to expand their interaction with AfD supporters, noting that entire villages are now divided. Maybe through local sports clubs, someone suggests? No, says another. Politics are unwelcome at sports clubs.
In the end, the group agrees to the proposal to remove the right-wing stickers. After that: We’ll see.
In eastern Germany, the AfD is no longer just part of public life, it is the main driver. It does what one-time SPD chair Sigmar Gabriel demanded from his party more that a decade-and-a-half ago: "We have to get out into the world! Where it’s loud, where it’s seething. Where it sometimes smells and sometimes stinks!”
That, too, isn’t exactly a strategy. But it is an additional element in the AfD plan.
A Media Foothold
Another element is the establishment of a discreet debate space isolated from traditional media. This includes Telegram channels and profiles on Facebook and Instagram, but also podcasts and local party newspapers. Beyond that, the extreme right-wing, party-affiliated media scene has now even established a presence in the Bundestag.
When the new parliament came together for its first session in late March, a right-wing online magazine set up its own stand right next to the public broadcaster Phoenix. Called the Deutschland Kurier, its motto – "Homeland. Identity. Freedom” – was clearly visible beneath its logo, the head of an eagle. The activists reported live from the plenary session on their YouTube channel and interviewed AfD parliamentarians.
The AfD is hoping that such coverage will continually shift the public discourse to the right – and bring public opinion along with it. The Italian Marxist Antonio Gramsci once wrote of the "cultural hegemony” that a movement must achieve if it wants to gain power. It is a message the AfD has understood.
"The AfD has come along way with this approach, in part because other parties have adopted some of its topics and narratives,” says right-wing extremism expert and sociologist Matthias Quent, who teaches at the Magdeburg-Stendal University of Applied Sciences.
For years, the party has been trying to exert pressure on cultural projects and pro-democracy programs, in part by using its position in state parliaments to query state governments about the non-profit and funding status of such projects. According to the public broadcaster MDR, AfD parliamentarians submitted 36 such queries from January to September 2024, looking for details a about the financing of cultural facilities and non-profit associations in the state of Saxony.
At the same time, says Quent, the AfD is careful to present itself as a normal political force, as a party that takes care of its constituents. "In some regions of eastern Germany, the AfD has almost achieved hegemony,” he says.
Things haven’t progressed that far in Berlin yet, but the AfD in the city-state has charted an even more radical course. In January, the party introduced a bill in the city parliament called "Strengthening Cultural Identity” – a title reminiscent of the Reichskulturkammer under the Nazi dictatorship.
Cultural funding in Berlin, the AfD bill proposed, should be structured such that "public money be used to a greater degree for the staging of classical plays in productions true to the original.” Meanwhile, "modern interpretations” should be increasingly measured against "transparent criteria such as their broader public appeal and cultural relevance.” The aim should be to "promote German cultural heritage and protect it from ideological transformation.”
From there, it’s not too large of a step to the Nazi concept of "degenerate art.” One of the co-signers of the motion was Ronald Gläser, who was the parliamentary secretary of the AfD group in Berlin city-state parliament before moving to the Bundestag in late March.
The cultural vanguard of the AfD includes YouTubers, publishing houses and TikTok accounts, along with right-wing extremist intellectuals like Götz Kubitschek. Just how large that vanguard has become will be on full display later this year in Halle, where the Neue Rechte will be gathering in early November for their very first book fair. Organizers are expecting more than 50 exhibitors spread out across 3,000 square meters of floorspace.
The organizer of the book fair is Susanne Dagen, a bookshop owner in Dresden who is also on the city council, where she joined the AfD fraction. Dagen is an old friend of the right-wing extremist Kubitschek and has discussed books on YouTube for years with his wife, Ellen Kositza.
Dagen denies that the book fair in Halle is intended to offer the right wing a place to meet up. There have been no arrangements made with political parties, she says, which anyway, in her view, have no "connection to literature.” The problem, she insists, is that the book fairs in Frankfurt and Leipzig have become "increasingly narrow politically.” As such, she views her book fair in Halle as an act of "intellectual self-defense.”
It is the same narrative one hears from the AfD: They constantly claim they are being marginalized and shoved to the fringes. Yet the AfD has a louder voice in the public debate than ever before. In Saxony-Anhalt, where Halle is located, the party is hoping to win state elections and produce Germany’s first-ever AfD governor.
In the February federal elections, the AfD won every single electoral district in Saxony-Anhalt and received over 37 percent of the vote – against just 19 percent for the CDU and well under 5 percent for the Greens and the Free Democrats. There is even a possibility that the state AfD chapter in Saxony-Anhalt, led by Martin Reichardt, could end up with an absolute majority, which would give the right-wing extremists a free hand politically.
Only the state’s CDU governor, Reiner Haseloff, the longest serving governor in the country, can likely prevent such an outcome. It is the same situation that has recently been seen ahead of election campaigns in a number of eastern German states: A popular governor from the political center fighting a more or less solitary battle against the AfD. The question is whether it will be enough this time around as well.
Inroads in the West
One of the myths that is often told about the AfD is that they are strong in places where people aren’t used to migration, particularly in eastern Germany. But now, in the Ruhr Valley of all places, the industrial region made powerful through immigration, there has been an AfD enclave since February: Gelsenkirchen. A quarter of all voters here cast their ballots for the AfD in February, and there is no shortage of voices arguing that it was just the beginning.
It is Wednesday of last week and Axel Büttner is sitting in front of a cup of tea in a parish hall in the Scholven district of Gelsenkirchen. He says he is "afraid of the approaching municipal elections and that we will have an AfD mayor by the end of the year.” The 68-year-old Büttner is a deacon – and he sounds almost desperate: "There are so many good things about this district. Enough elementary schools, a number of facilities for children and youth, plenty of supermarkets.” But every third vote in Scholven went to the AfD.
The problem facing all of Gelsenkirchen is poverty. In the early 1960s, the city was a proud coal metropolis, home to almost 400,000 people. Today, Gelsenkirchen has a population of just 270,000, with around 75,000 of them lacking a German passport, and it has become Germany’s low-income capital. Nowhere in Germany is the jobless rate higher and almost every second child faces poverty. Every sixth resident is carrying excessive debt.
There are nice areas in the city with parks, beautiful 19th century residential buildings and newer developments where the mines once were. But you don’t have to go far to find piles of discarded furniture in front of vacant, boarded up homes. Büttner is often out and about in the district on his bicycle. "Before the last election, I didn’t see a single AfD campaign sign. The party is invisible here,” he says.
Apparently, there was no need for the AfD to mount much of a campaign.
Indeed, this is likely the most important element in the AfD’s plan: the widespread frustration people feel about the condition in which the country currently finds itself – frustration that is not just present in places like Gelsenkirchen, where the anger and disappointment are more than justified, but also in places where people are actually doing quite well.
The plan calls for declaring every annoyance, every bit of adversity experienced in everyday life, as a failure of the system: waiting times to see a doctor, train delays, filthy restrooms in schools. Germany’s centrist parties, according to the AfD narrative, are unable to get such problems under control and it is time to try something else. To amplify this narrative, to make it even more horrific, the AfD deploys its tried-and-true toolbox of manipulation, half-truths and outright lies.
That is something the Union and the SPD hope to stand up to over the next four years. "We have to be successful,” is how Markus Söder – the governor of Bavaria and head of the Christian Social Union (CSU) – put it recently as the Union and SPD gathered to begin the process of putting the finishing touches on their coalition. The new government, he said, must be strong enough to "ensure the growth of a bit more appreciation and respect for our democracy.”
Politicians from both sides of the aisle have been concerned by the fact that even though the Union and SPD recently pushed through a gigantic infrastructure and defense spending bill – even before finalizing their coalition – the AfD has continued to rise in the public opinion polls. The SPD believes it is a function of the radical U-turn performed by Friedrich Merz. During the campaign, Merz pledged to avoid taking on new debt and provided no clear answers as to how he intended to finance better equipment for the German military and fund overdue infrastructure renovations. Only to then take on more debt than ever as soon as the votes were counted.
That has led to a situation, the SPD argues, in which many people are unable to recognize the benefits of that spending bill – the improvements it promises for the country – and to see only the blatant jettisoning of campaign promises. In doing so, the argument continues, Merz has substantiated the AfD narrative according to which the so-called establishment parties cannot be trusted.
The Union, meanwhile, is hoping that time is on their side and that people will begin to realize that things actually are improving. In addition to a new approach to migration, Merz and his team are primarily putting their eggs in the economic growth basket. Once people again have more money in their wallets and don’t have to worry about losing their jobs, the rise of the AfD will stop. They hope.
Bernd Baumann, a senior AfD member in German parliament, rejects that argument. "The CDU and the SPD still believe that economic factors contribute to the rise of the AfD. But it is primarily due to the massive socio-cultural changes in our country, mostly caused by uncontrolled migration,” he says. If the Union continues its policy of open borders "and people recognize their city districts even less in four years, the CDU will be punished for good. Then, it will be our time.”
The borders, it should be noted, are no longer open. But the AfD continues making the claim anyway.
The right-wingers are also getting a boost from the zeitgeist, which is drifting further and further to the right, and not just in Germany. Liberal democracy is under pressure around the world and authoritarianism is having its day in the sun. In the U.S., Donald Trump is in the White House, while in France, the political center is worried about right-wing populist Marine Le Pen. A court there recently ruled that Le Pen is not allowed to take part in the 2027 presidential election, but she is battling that ruling in the hopes of being able to run anyway.
An Important Opportunity for the Political Center
The debate in Germany over the possible banning of the AfD, meanwhile, is likely to continue as well. In the last legislative period, more than 100 members of German parliament tried to file a petition for the Constitutional Court to consider a ban, but they were ultimately unable to find a majority for their cross-party effort.
Those in favor of such a ban hope things might change if the Federal Office for the Protection of the Constitution(BfV) designates the federal AfD party as right-wing extremist. Thus far, the party has only been classified as a suspected case of right-wing extremism, an important legal distinction. Months could pass before the BfV ratchets up the pressure on the party, and the AfD will try to take advantage of the time available to it.
In parliament, meanwhile, the AfD will likely find it difficult to make much progress. Thus far, at least, the other parties have maintained a solid front against the right. During the inaugural session in late March, when the vice presidents of the Bundestag are elected, the AfD candidate Gerold Otten failed to get elected three times in what is usually a mere formality (given that each party in the Bundestag gets one vice president). Subsequent efforts are likely to end the same way.
The next task for the Bundestag is setting up the committees and choosing their chairs. As the strongest opposition party, tradition holds that the AfD is entitled to the chair of the Budget Committee. "Denying us that would be quite a thing,” says a source close to AfD floor leader Alice Weidel. But it sounds more helpless than anything. During the last legislative session, the AfD didn’t end up with a single committee chair – and the party believes the same thing could happen again this time around.
"The firewall works. Why would the others want to change anything?” wonders a staffer for a western German AfD representative. He doesn’t have too many ideas when it comes to what he thinks his party might be able to attain with its newfound strength. "It has no strategy,” he says in annoyance, "and hasn’t for years now.”
It is here where the grand AfD plan encounters its limits – precisely where the AfD should formulate its own political vision and chart a proactive course, instead of relying on the weakness of the others, voter frustration and the right-wing zeitgeist. It is a gaping hole in the plan. And a sign of hope for liberal democracy.
It is said that AfD leaders in parliament are currently working on a grand strategy paper. But behind the scenes of the federal party, some are concerned that the party may not actually have the political substance to justify the 20.8 percent it received in the last election. And that more growth, at least at the federal level, may not be likely.
There is a lack of a political epicenter say party members, adding that while Weidel, the party’s chancellor candidate during the campaign, and her co-floor leader Tino Chrupalla managed to team up on the stump, that alliance has now come to an end. Chrupalla, it is said in the party, is now trying to raise his profile. He declined to comment for this story.
The AfD must accept that there is a significant gap between its dominance in some regions – like Saxony-Anhalt, Brandenburg and Gelsenkirchen – and the mood in Berlin. In the German capital, some in the party have begun to realize that the next few years could be difficult – particularly if the Union and the SPD manage to boost the country’s rather dark mood.
Party leaders and senior AfD parliamentarians are fully aware that they won’t be moving into the Chancellery any time soon. They do, though, want to at least make waves in the capital and make sure that here, in the center of German political power, nobody forgets about them.
Thus far, the AfD federal headquarters have been located in northern Berlin, right in the middle of an industrial park. But rumors have recently been flying in the top echelons of the party that the AfD is interested in moving its headquarters to the center of the city, and perhaps even buying its own piece of property. The location on the northern edge of the city, with long travel times to the government district and the heating plant nearby, "no longer fits us. It makes it look as though we were far away from the action,” says a confidant of Alice Weidel.
Carsten Hütter, the party’s federal treasurer, declines to comment on potential plans for a move, but he does recall a decision the party made some time ago to buy property. He says he "still feels bound” by that decision.
The AfD likely has sufficient money to do so, having grown wealthier and wealthier in recent years, in part by inheriting money from private citizens. The current statement of accounts lists net assets of 38.3 million euros. In the meantime, however, that sum is likely to have grown significantly higher.
